card.hook: Check the doorway: it's not in the middle, and that wonky confidence is what makes this front so fun. Rows of diamond-cut limestone do the rest, like a giant stone pattern made for your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza de España, directly in front of the main facade. The front looks west across the square, so face the palace and you'll fit the whole thing in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the full facade. If you can't fit the top balconies in, tap 0.5x, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for close-ups of the diamond stonework and the doorway.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stone wall, then slide it a touch darker if the pale limestone looks washed out against the sky.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is reportedly lovely, when the low western sun lights the stonework (that's from one blog, so treat it as a tip, not a promise).
card.selfie_here: Try the staircase in the inner courtyard, with the palace stonework around you. It's only an old forum anecdote (couples had wedding photos taken there), so don't count on it. Use the front camera, and 0.5x if you want more stone in the shot.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to someone at the far end of Calle Mayor, where the street meets the palace front, while you stand in the square in front of the facade.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the facade from the square. The palace is also the Museum of Guadalajara, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
card.challenge: Take one straight-on shot, then step to the side and take another, and see if the diamond points suddenly look deeper.
card.good_to_know: This 15th-century palace is built in the Isabelline style and was once the seat of the Dukes of the Infantado. It has been protected as a Bien de Interés Cultural since 1914. It was damaged in the Spanish Civil War, and since 1973 it has housed the Museum of Guadalajara.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plaza de España, directly in front of the main facade. The front looks west across the square, so face the palace and you'll fit the whole thing in one frame.

selfie_spots.why: A 2012 wedding-forum poster called the smaller patio's staircase very attractive, and said couples had their photos taken there, though this is an anecdote rather than a selfie guide.

card.hook: A bright purple dome rising over a school campus is not something you expect to find on a walk through a park, and that's why this spot is so much fun. You see it from across the Parque de San Roque, and it's hard to miss.
card.stand_here: Head into Parque de San Roque, on the entrance side of the pantheon. The building is about 3 minutes on foot from there. Face the pantheon's approach with the building to the south, so the entrance, dome and roofs all sit in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole entrance and dome, with a strip of park in front. Then try 2x to get close to the purple tiles and the stonework. Only use 0.5x if you're close, and hold your phone level so the edges don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the entrance on the centre line and check the roof sits straight, because this building is symmetrical and it shows.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stone and the dome than midday. If the sky is very bright, drag the brightness slider down a little so the purple keeps its colour.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the park ground next to the pantheon and face away from it with the dome as your backdrop. Use the front camera and hold it a bit low, so the dome fits over your shoulder. No page gives an exact standing point, so wander a few steps until the dome sits nicely behind you.
card.ask_someone: If the porch of the Ermita de San Roque is open, ask a passer-by to stand there and take your picture with the whole pantheon in view.
card.rules_and_safety: The pantheon stands inside a school campus, so take your photos from the public park or street side. Photos are not allowed inside the pantheon.
card.challenge: Get the entrance dead centre on the gridlines with the dome right above it, then see if you can do the same with yourself in the shot.
card.good_to_know: Ricardo Velázquez Bosco designed this funerary building for María Diega Desmaissières y Sevillano, known locally as the Duchess of Sevillano. Permission was granted in June 1887 and work finished in 1916, the year she died. It's built on a Greek cross plan, with Novelda stone walls and that purple-tiled dome.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head into Parque de San Roque, on the entrance side of the pantheon. The building is about 3 minutes on foot from there. Face the pantheon's approach with the building to the south, so the entrance, dome and roofs all sit in front of you.

selfie_spots.why: The dome is the city's best-known landmark and the park lies right beside it, so the visitor can face outward with the pantheon behind.

card.hook: Here's a fun one: you're about to photograph a palace that spends its weekdays full of schoolkids. The Palace of Antonio de Mendoza in Guadalajara sits right beside the Piedad church, with a little open garden between them, so you get two historic buildings in one go.
card.stand_here: Stand on Calle Teniente Figueroa, opposite the garden entrance, on the street side of the palace front. The palace is to the south of you, so face it and you'll see the front, the balcony and the church portal across the garden.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the palace front, the garden and the church portal in one frame. If the pavement is too narrow to step back, try 0.5x, and keep your phone level so the walls don't lean. Then switch to 2x for a closer shot of the balcony.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the balcony on one of the third lines, and let the garden lead the eye across to the church.
card.best_time: Pick a moment when the street is quiet and the light is soft and even, like a bright but cloudy day or earlier in the day. If a car or passer-by wrecks your first shot, just wait a moment and go again.
card.selfie_here: Step into the open garden between the palace and the church and face out to the street, with the palace front behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze more building in, and keep the palace over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pavement across from the garden, facing the palace, while you stand in the garden with the palace behind you, so the doorway, balcony and church all fit in.
card.rules_and_safety: The palace is a working school, so the courtyard inside isn't an open public space. Check the official site before you go if you hope to see inside.
card.challenge: Take the same shot twice, once with the whole street scene and once at 2x with just the balcony, then see which one you like better.
card.good_to_know: The palace has been protected as a Bien de Interés Cultural, Spain's heritage listing, since 1931. It is still a secondary school today, IES Liceo Caracense. You'll find it at number 6 on Calle Teniente Figueroa, though it may also show up as number 8, so check on the day.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Calle Teniente Figueroa, opposite the garden entrance, on the street side of the palace front. The palace is to the south of you, so face it and you'll see the front, the balcony and the church portal across the garden.

selfie_spots.detail: stand in the garden facing out to the street, with the palace front behind you
selfie_spots.why: The palace and the church together enclose a garden that opens onto the street, which gives an open, uncluttered background for a selfie.

Verify them on site. The building is a working secondary school (IES Liceo Caracense), and the patio is open only at set times: Saturdays 10:30–14:00 and 16:30–18:30 (17:00–19:00 in summer), and Sundays and holidays 10:30–14:00. Entry is free. One Ayuntamiento page lists 'Plaza Mayor 7' as the directions address, which conflicts with the Calle Teniente Figueroa 6 address given on every other source; I used Teniente Figueroa 6. The coordinates you gave match the Wikipedia listing (40.634822, -3.166734). No page states rules on selfie sticks or tripods, and no page gives a safety point, so those fields are empty.

card.hook: This little brick chapel looks like a castle that shrank in the wash: round corner turrets, crenellations on top and deep eaves tucked underneath. It's small, so a short stop is enough to get a great photo.
card.stand_here: Stand in front of the Concatedral de Santa María in central Guadalajara. The chapel is to the north-east, about 78 m away, so face north-east and look across to it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x from the cathedral frontage to fit the chapel and the church in one shot. Then use 2x to home in on the corner turrets and crenellations.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines, line the chapel walls up with the vertical lines so the brick doesn't lean, and tap the brick wall so it keeps its colour even if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Soft daylight is kind to brick. Harsh midday sun can wash out the colour and turn the shadows under the eaves very dark.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x to fit more in, and hold the phone a bit higher and further out. Turn so the chapel's brick walls sit over your shoulder, then check the turrets aren't hidden behind your head.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the outside from the street. If you want to go inside, check the official site before you go, as opening is limited.
card.challenge: Take two shots of the same chapel: one wide from the cathedral, then one close-up of a turret. Which one would you frame?
card.good_to_know: The chapel is also known as the Capilla de las Urbinas. It was declared a Bien de Interés Cultural in 1914, which is Spain's formal heritage protection. It stands opposite the Concatedral de Santa María, and the sloping Cuesta de San Miguel leads up to it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in front of the Concatedral de Santa María in central Guadalajara. The chapel is to the north-east, about 78 m away, so face north-east and look across to it.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found recommends a selfie spot or a photo position for this chapel, so I am not naming any. Pages found: a Guadalajara council tourist guide (guadalajara.es PDF) gives the chapel's location on Cuesta de San Miguel and notes an exterior route without difficulties; the Senderismo Guadalajara page (senderismoguadalajara.es) gives the address Cuesta de San Miguel, 7 and says the chapel sits opposite the co-cathedral of Santa María; spain.info gives the address Cuesta de San Miguel, s/n. Tripadvisor reviews mention a spiral staircase for viewing the ceiling frescoes, which is an indoor viewing tip rather than a photo spot. The Wikimedia Commons photos have coordinates matching the given position, but they are not guides. Because the co-cathedral is named as opposite the chapel, a visitor could test a photo in front of the chapel with the co-cathedral in view, but that is my inference, not something a source recommends, so I have left it out. No page I found covers selfie sticks, tripods, or safety for this site. Another search for a Guadalajara selfie or photo-spot guide, or a local blog, might find a named spot.

card.hook: San Ginés doesn't need any fuss: one heavy stone front, two big buttresses and two belfry towers, and you get the whole building at a glance. That makes it a gift for a phone.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza de Santo Domingo, the open square the church stands on, and face the church. From here you get an angled view, which still looks good. For the full front, walk round to the west side of the square so you can step back far enough.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x. Switch to 0.5x only if the square is too crowded to step back, and keep the building in the middle so the edges don't stretch. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for a close-up of a belfry.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the buttresses up with the vertical lines, so the towers stand straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Go when the sky is bright but even, like a light overcast day or a clear morning. The stone looks great without harsh shadows. Planning to go inside, or visiting very early or late? Check the church's opening times first.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the open paving in Plaza de Santo Domingo, in front of the church, with the church behind you. Use the front camera, and if your phone has a 0.5x button on it, try that to fit more of the building over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working parish church, so be discreet if people are coming and going. Wait for a gap rather than asking anyone to move.
card.challenge: Can you get both belfry towers sitting evenly on either side of your frame? Take a few steps left or right until they match.
card.good_to_know: San Ginés is a working parish church in Guadalajara. It was declared a Bien de Interés Cultural in 1931, which is Spain's heritage protection for important buildings. Its main facade faces west. For a quieter angle, Plaza Pablo Iglesias is nearby, but check the framing on the day.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plaza de Santo Domingo, the open square the church stands on, and face the church. From here you get an angled view, which still looks good. For the full front, walk round to the west side of the square so you can step back far enough.

card.hook: Most people shoot this bridge from the top of the path, and the arches end up looking small and far away. Walk down toward the water and they rise right in front of you, which is much more fun.
card.stand_here: Stand in Parque del Río Henares, on the left-hand side of the riverside footpath as you go down toward the water. Face the bridge so the arches rise above you, with a bit of water in front.
card.zoom: Start at 1x and try to fit the whole bridge in. Switch to 0.5x if you're close to the water and want several arches in one shot, then go to 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for a tight shot of two or three arches and their reflections.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the line of the arches on the lower or upper third, and tap the arches so they stay sharp.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives soft light that suits stone and water. Check the light on the day, because the sun's position changes with the season.
card.selfie_here: Use the riverside path right next to the bridge's arches, with the bridge behind you. Switch to the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the arches over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by and pose on the new bridge, Nuevo puente del Henares, where the old bridge is in view on one side.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge is open to pedestrians and the riverside park is a public space, but check the official site before you go in case of local closures or works.
card.challenge: If the water is calm, catch the arches in their reflection and see whether you can make one perfect circle from arch plus mirror image.
card.good_to_know: The Bridge of Henares was built in the 10th century and widened after the Reconquista, so its stonework carries several centuries of history. It's 117 metres long. It has been a protected Bien de Interés Cultural since 1931.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Parque del Río Henares, on the left-hand side of the riverside footpath as you go down toward the water. Face the bridge so the arches rise above you, with a bit of water in front.

card.hook: Most churches show off. This one hides its best bits behind a plain brick wall and a flight of steps that dips down below the street. That modesty is exactly why it makes such a nice photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on Calle Teniente Figueroa, opposite the church front, on the side you reach by walking up from the Palacio del Infantado along Calle Mayor. The church is to the west of this point, so face the brick south façade and the stone portal.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the whole façade and the narrow street into one frame. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x for the stone portal and the brick texture.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the portal up with a vertical line so the walls don't lean, then tap the portal and slide it a touch darker if the bright sky is making the brick look dull.
card.best_time: Go in daylight, when the brick shows its warm colour. Soft morning or late-afternoon light is a nice bet.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at 0.5x, hold the phone a little higher than your face, and tuck the brick front over your shoulder. Check the doorway isn't sprouting out of your head before you tap.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a place of worship, so respect any services, and check opening hours and any works on the building before you visit. The apse is the prettiest side, but it's seen from the rectory courtyard, which isn't public, so stick to the street view.
card.challenge: Take two shots: a wide one that shows the church in its street, then a close one of the portal against the brick. Bonus points if the entrance steps make it into the first one.
card.good_to_know: The Church of Santiago el Mayor dates from the 14th century and has been a Bien de Interés Cultural since 1946. The calm exterior hides a Gothic-Mudéjar interior, and the nave sits below street level, which is why the steps are part of the scene. Walking up from the Palacio del Infantado, the church comes into view on your left.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Calle Teniente Figueroa, opposite the church front, on the side you reach by walking up from the Palacio del Infantado along Calle Mayor. The church is to the west of this point, so face the brick south façade and the stone portal.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with the church behind, or a passer-by spot for photographing a visitor with the whole church, so both lists are empty rather than guessed. The search returned mostly Tripadvisor photo captions and Wikimedia Commons files, which give no viewpoints. Possible leads only, not verified as photo spots: (1) Divento says the church is almost guarded by a statue of Commander Don Gonzalo de Ulloa, but it gives no position or photo advice. (2) Tripadvisor photo captions mention a double staircase at a lateral entrance and stairs down to the church, and Urbipedia says the interior sits below street level. Neither gives a standing point outside. Addresses conflict: Tripadvisor gives Calle Teniente Figueroa 1, while Urbipedia gives Calle Miguel Fluiters 26; the Urbipedia coordinates match the position you supplied. Rules and safety: no page I found states selfie stick or tripod rules, or a safety point for this church.

card.hook: Most people stroll past this front in a few seconds, and that's a shame, because it rewards a slower look. Brick, stone, two coats of arms and a doorway are all waiting to be spotted, even if you've only got a minute.
card.stand_here: Stand on Calle Ingeniero Mariño, right in front of the church facade (the phone icon on the map is at the building itself). Face the church so the whole front is ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole facade in. If the street is too narrow to fit it all, drop to 0.5x and keep the building away from the edges of the frame, where it can look stretched. Then go to 2x or higher (depending on your phone) for the coats of arms and the doorway.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edges of the facade with them so the building doesn't lean, then tap the brick wall and slide a bit darker if the sky is bright so the stonework keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go in daylight, when the brick and stone detail is clear. Check the light on the day, because the street may be partly in shade.
card.selfie_here: Try Plaza Beatas Mártires, at its corner with Calle Ingeniero Mariño, where one guide places the convent corner. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it), hold it a little higher and keep the convent over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pavement of Calle Ingeniero Mariño facing the church door, while you stand in front of the door, so the whole facade with its coats of arms fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The approach to the entrance is on a slope, so find level footing before you frame the shot. The inside may be closed, so plan on the outside as your photo and check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find all three coats of arms: one on each side of the doorway, and the Carmelite arms above the convent door. Get a close-up of each one!
card.good_to_know: This is a Carmelite convent in Guadalajara, near the co-cathedral. The Baroque front is built of brick and stone. It was declared a Bien de Interés Cultural in 1992.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Calle Ingeniero Mariño, right in front of the church facade (the phone icon on the map is at the building itself). Face the church so the whole front is ahead of you.

selfie_spots.detail: on the plaza at the corner where the convent stands, with the convent corner behind you
selfie_spots.why: One guide places the convent on this corner, so a visitor standing on the plaza has the building behind them.

card.hook: Brick and stone don't usually get along this well. At the Church of San Nicolás, a pale carved Baroque doorway sits in a warm brick front, and your phone loves the contrast.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Plaza del Jardinillo, across the square from the church's brick front, with the Banco de España building beside it in the same view. Face the church and step back until you can fit the doorway and the top of the facade without tilting your phone upwards.
card.zoom: Zoom 1x is right for most people, and it gets the whole front with some square in the foreground. For a closer shot of the stone doorway, try zoom 2x instead of walking closer. Zoom 0.5x can squeeze in the bank too, but it stretches the edges, so keep the church in the middle.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the edges of the facade straight, then tap the brick and slide it a touch darker if the sky is bright so the brick keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go when the sun is lighting the front of the church rather than leaving it in shade. A quieter square means fewer strangers wandering through your picture.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and hold your phone slightly above eye level. Switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, so the church fits over your shoulder, then check that the doorway isn't hidden behind your head.
card.rules_and_safety: The outside is on a public square. If you want to go in, check the opening hours first, as the church may be closed at times.
card.challenge: Line up the doorway in the middle of the gridlines and get the brick-to-stone edges perfectly straight. Bonus point if the Banco de España building sneaks into one side of the frame.
card.good_to_know: The church stands on the edge of the Plaza del Jardinillo in Guadalajara, Spain. Its main facade is brick, with a stone Baroque doorway set into it. It was declared a Bien de Interés Cultural in 1981, which is Spain's formal heritage protection for important buildings.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the Plaza del Jardinillo, across the square from the church's brick front, with the Banco de España building beside it in the same view. Face the church and step back until you can fit the doorway and the top of the facade without tilting your phone upwards.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot or a spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole church, so both fields are empty rather than guessed. The only named location is Plaza del Jardinillo, where the church stands (Tripadvisor listing, https://www.tripadvisor.com/LocationPhotoDirectLink-g262063-d2254431-i39979668-Church_of_San_Nicolas-Guadalajara_Province_of_Guadalajara_Castile_La_Manc.html; Brújula Viajera, https://brujulaviajera.com/que-ver-en-guadalajara/; Kris por el mundo, https://www.krisporelmundo.com/que-ver-en-guadalajara/). A SkyscraperCity photo caption (https://www.skyscrapercity.com/threads/guadalajara.496957/page-5) describes the plaza with the Banco de España building on the left and the church on the right, but gives no standing point, so I did not use it as a spot. The church's official address is C/ Mayor, 21 (https://www.guadalajara.es/es/actividad-economica/iglesia-de-san-nicolas-.html). Searching the square's name plus 'fotos' or 'mirador' might surface a blog that names a specific spot. The site is also called San Nicolás el Real in some sources; I did not find any selfie-stick or tripod rule or any safety point on these pages.

card.hook: Most churches hide down a narrow street, so you end up photographing one tiny slice of wall. This one gets a whole square to itself, and its warm brick front looks great for it.
card.stand_here: Stand on Plaza de Santa María, right in front of the main facade, and face the church. Step back until the arched doorway and the tower beside it both fit on your screen.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the doorway and tower together. If the tower gets chopped off, tap 0.5x. For a closer look at the horseshoe-shaped arch, tap 2x. Keep your phone upright so the tower stays tall.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines to keep the vertical lines of the facade straight, then tap the brickwork and slide darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day, when the brick looks warm and the facade is evenly lit. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light, but check on the day which light actually reaches the front.
card.selfie_here: Head for the open paving of Plaza de Santa María and stand with the brick church behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold your phone a little low so the facade rises over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a place of worship, so check the official site for visiting arrangements before you go if you want to see inside. The square itself is an open public space.
card.challenge: Can you get the horseshoe arch, the tower and a bit of open square all in one straight-lined shot?
card.good_to_know: The Co-cathedral of Santa María la Mayor is built in the Mudéjar style, a blend of Christian and Islamic building traditions. You can spot that mix in the horseshoe-shaped arch over the main doorway. It's one of the seats of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Sigüenza-Guadalajara, and it was declared a Bien de Interés Cultural, Spain's heritage listing, on 12 July 1941.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Plaza de Santa María, right in front of the main facade, and face the church. Step back until the arched doorway and the tower beside it both fit on your screen.

selfie_spots.name: Plaza de Santa María, open paving in front of the church's brick facade
selfie_spots.detail: stand in the open part of the square with the brick church behind you (exact stance is my inference; the source doesn't specify one)
selfie_spots.why: The regional tourism page calls the square a strong spot for urban photos, and its brick Mudéjar facade is the main subject.

selfie_research.notes: The search results were mostly about Guadalajara, Mexico, and I excluded them. The coordinates match the Spanish co-cathedral (Plaza de Santa María 5, Guadalajara, Spain). Only one Spanish tourism page names a photo location, and it gives no selfie stance, so the selfie spot above is a plaza-level suggestion, not a precise stand-point. No page I found names a spot for a passer-by to photograph the visitor with the whole church in frame, so I left ask_someone_spot null. An espanaviajar.com page says the co-cathedral was named partly after a water fountain across from its front, but no page recommends that fountain for photos, so I did not use it. No page gave selfie-stick, tripod, or safety rules for this site.

card.hook: This stone tower sits on a slope, so its arched openings end up on different sides, and that quirk is why it looks so good from the park below. Look up and let the garden terraces do the rest.
card.stand_here: Stand in Parque de la Huerta de San Antonio, in the lower park below the tower's west side. The tower is to the north-east, so face that way and look up at it over the garden terraces, with the Infantado palace area behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the tower and the terraces into one frame. Switch to 1x for a tidier, less stretched look at the stonework, and try 2x to 5x (if your phone has them) for the arches and masonry.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower, then slide a little darker if the sky is bright so the stone keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon tends to be kind to stonework, but that's a rule of thumb, so go when it suits you and check how the stone looks on your screen. Come when the park is quiet if you can.
card.selfie_here: Try the park path at the tower's western edge, near the double-arched doorway that leads to the lower floor. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and turn so the tower rises over your shoulder, then check your screen to make sure it's in the shot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by at the crossing of Calle Alvarfáñez de Minaya and Avenida del Ejército, facing the linear park, so the tower is in front of them and you're in the picture.
card.rules_and_safety: The lower-floor entrance from the park is steep, so take care on the slope. If you want to go inside the tower, check the official site first, as visiting rules may apply.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, put the tower on a vertical line with the terraces filling the bottom third, and see if you can keep the stone walls looking straight.
card.good_to_know: The tower is pentagonal, up to 14 metres high, and once formed part of Guadalajara's medieval defences. It's named after Álvar Fáñez, an 11th-century Leonese nobleman and lieutenant of El Cid. It became a Bien de Interés Cultural in 1921, was fully refurbished in 2004, and now holds an exhibition on the origins of the city's coat of arms and the legend of Álvar Fáñez.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Parque de la Huerta de San Antonio, in the lower park below the tower's west side. The tower is to the north-east, so face that way and look up at it over the garden terraces, with the Infantado palace area behind.

selfie_spots.name: Parque de la Huerta de San Antonio, on the park path at the foot of the tower
selfie_spots.detail: on the park path at the tower's western edge, near the double-arched doorway that leads to the lower floor
selfie_spots.why: Guides and photo pages show the tower rising above this Arab-style garden, so a visitor standing in the park can have the tower behind them.
